agree.reason: The update opens with a plain apology, gives the real reason for the silence, sets a dated commitment, offers monthly numbers and makes two small, concrete requests, so a cold lead investor is likely to take the call, though they may still worry that there is no plan for the runway.

honest.reason: Most claims match the facts, but 'I haven't decided whether to raise more money or cut costs' and 'I don't yet know how many of our clinics overall use a records system with its own scheduler' are statements the founder never made.

works_the_facts.reason: It works out about 11 months of runway and $900/month if all six reminder buyers follow through, and it explains that new sales replaced the lost revenue, but it never shows the at-risk $3,800 as about 9% of MRR, the lost chain as about 13% of MRR, or the drop in no-shows as nearly half.

right_comparison.reason: It says growth went into replacing lost revenue, but it never spells out what happens if nothing changes: flat revenue with cash running out around next October, and another $3,800 likely to leave the same way.

qualification.reason: The reminder launch is hedged with a number ($900 if all six buy), a date (report on January 7) and a test of whether reminders sell on their own, but it doesn't say what the founder will conclude or do if fewer than six convert.

objections.reason: It answers the investor's complaint about missed updates directly, with an apology, the reason and a dated commitment to fix it, and it is upfront about the risk from the records system, though by presenting cash strategy as undecided it invites the question 'what is your plan?'

fit.reason: At about 450 words it is under the limit and well organised as an investor update, but it leaves [Company] and [Your name] as placeholders even though Cadence Scheduling and Sam Patel were known.
